teaser: Munich laughed at horses painted blue. The painter had a precise reason.

lesson.text: Munich, December 1911. In three rooms of a private gallery, a new group with an odd name, the Blue Rider, hangs its first exhibition. Visitors find a cow painted yellow, a deer painted red, and this: three horses the color of deep water. Much of the local press treated the show as a joke or an insult.

To those visitors, a painter had one job with a horse: get the coat right. Chestnut, bay, gray. Franz Marc could do that perfectly well. He had studied animal anatomy for years and even taught it to other artists. The blue was a decision, not a mistake.
The group's name came out of a conversation at a garden table. As Wassily Kandinsky later told it, both men loved blue, Marc loved horses and Kandinsky loved riders. So: the Blue Rider.

A year before the show, Marc had written to his painter friend August Macke and laid out a private code. Blue stood for the masculine: severe and spiritual. Yellow stood for the feminine: gentle, cheerful, sensual. Red stood for matter: heavy, brutal, the color the other two must fight and overcome.
For Marc, color was no longer a description of a thing's surface. It was a statement about its inner nature, the way a key signature sets the mood of a piece of music.

With that code in hand, the picture reads differently. Three spiritual creatures stand in a world of red, heavy matter. But Marc does something more with the red hills: he makes them rhyme with the animals.
Trace the backs of the horses, then the land behind them.

lines.label: First arc
lines.text: The nearest horse bows its head to the left. Its neck and mane form one round curve, dark on top like a brushed eyebrow.

lines.label: Second arc
lines.text: The horse on the right curls the same way, its neck folding down toward its own chest. Its back makes a long, low bridge.

lines.label: Third arc
lines.text: Behind them, the mane of a third horse repeats the curve one step higher.

lines.label: The hill
lines.text: And the red and violet hill on the horizon swells in the same rounded line. Animal and land are drawn with one gesture, as if made of the same stuff.

lesson.text: That echo is the real subject. Marc believed animals lived inside nature in a way people had lost, without standing apart to judge it. He wanted to paint the world as a horse might feel it, not as a rider sees it. So the bodies have no sharp edges, no fear, no sideways glance at us. They are folded into themselves like sleepers.
The trick that keeps all this roundness from going soft is a pair of pale tree trunks. They slice the picture from top to bottom, thin and white against the swollen blues.
Two details that keep the dream in order.

spots.title: The white trunk
spots.text: A slender trunk, likely a birch, sweeps down across the right horse in a long bow. It is the only cool, pale line among the curves, and it pins the horses into the landscape like a stitch.

spots.title: A lowered head
spots.text: Here the right horse tucks its head, with a pale blaze on its dark face. Its eye is shut or nearly so. None of the three horses looks outward.

spots.title: Yellow ground
spots.text: A patch of pure yellow at the horses' feet, with green leaves like blades. In Marc's code yellow is gentle and joyful: it lights the blues from below.

lesson.text: The canvas is wide, about 105 by 181 cm (41 by 71 inches), yet the horses barely fit. Marc cropped them on purpose so their bodies fill the view and you stand among them, not in front of them.

In 1942 the painting was bought by the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis, one of the first modern pictures the museum ever acquired. By then Marc had been dead for twenty-six years, killed near Verdun in 1916 at the age of thirty-six. The blue horse had become his signature, and that of a whole movement.

The visitors of 1911 asked why the horses were blue. Marc might have turned the question around. What color is calm? What color is something you trust? You probably have an answer, and it probably is not chestnut.

quiz.question: In Marc's private color code, what did blue stand for?
quiz.explanation: He set out the code in a letter to August Macke.

quiz.question: What do the curves of the horses' backs echo?
options: The red hill on the horizon
quiz.explanation: Animal and land are drawn with the same rounded line.

quiz.question: How did much of the Munich press react to the first Blue Rider exhibition?
quiz.explanation: Much of the local press treated it as a joke or an insult.

quiz.question: Why are the horses cropped by the edges of the canvas?
options: The canvas was cut down later
Marc ran out of room by accident
So that you stand among them
quiz.explanation: Marc filled the view with their bodies on purpose.

facts.text: Marc painted the horses blue because he had never studied real horses.
facts.explanation: He had studied animal anatomy for years and even taught it.

facts.text: In Marc's code, red stood for heavy matter that the other colors must overcome.
facts.explanation: Blue was spiritual, yellow gentle, red brutal and heavy.

facts.text: The three horses look out at the viewer.
facts.explanation: They are folded into themselves; none looks outward.
